newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Britain doubts nuclear test ban treaty, Australia confident.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Britain doubts nuclear test ban treaty, Australia confident.

text.p: British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo on Monday cast doubt over the final ratification of a global nuclear test ban treaty, even if the treaty is adopted by the United Nations this week.
But Australia was confident its U.N. resolution on the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) would be adopted, possibly as early as Tuesday, and that the treaty would come into force.
"Discussing it in the United Nations may help in indicating world opinion, but it will not in itself clinch the treaty," said Portillo in a video-linked press conference in Canberra.

Portillo said that there was still uncertainty on whether the treaty would be ratified as there was disagreement on how many nuclear and nuclear threshold states needed to sign the treaty to bring it into force, banning atmospheric and underground nuclear tests.
"When that was last discussed in Geneva (at the Conference for Disarmament) we were a little way short of a consensus," said Portillo, who is in Australia for defence talks.
Australia's U.N. Ambassador Richard Butler said he was confident the treaty would be ratified within its three year timeframe.
"This is not quite tablets of stone like Moses coming down from the mountain, but it's about as close as it gets in moral and political commitment in international law," Butler said.

Butler said all five nuclear weapon states would sign the CTBT in the United Nations immediately and that all 44 nations needed for ratification under the International Atomic Energy Agency rules would be eventually forthcoming.
Only India, a nuclear threshold state, has said it would not sign the treaty, according to Australia.

"With the great moral force that will build up behind this treaty I am not sure they (India) will end up being absent from it at the end of that (three year) time," Butler told Australian Broadcasting Corporation radio from New York.
Australia says it has 121 countries ready to co-sponsor its U.N. resolution out of a general assembly of 185 nations.
An Australian foreign affairs department official said the U.N. General Assembly would discuss the resolution on Monday, New York time, and possibly vote as early as Tuesday.
If the resolution were adopted, the CTBT treaty could be signed on September 24, she said.

After nearly three years of negotiations for a CTBT, India in August vetoed the draft treaty because it allows the five declared nuclear powers to refine their nuclear arsenals through laboratory computer simulated tests. The draft also failed to commit them to a timetable for total disarmament.

India also said it opposed a clause that would require its signature to ratify the pact. New Delhi, which exploded a nuclear device in 1974 but has denied possessing atomic weapons, said the measure impinged on its sovereignty.
The five nuclear states are Britain, the United States, Russia, China and France, with India, Pakistan and Israel known as the three threshold states.
Australia said a successful vote on the CTBT would bolster its candidature for a U.N. Security Council seat.
The U.N. Security Council has five permanent seats, taken by the United States, Britain, Russia, France, China, and 10 non-permanent seats, which are held for two years.
Australia, which has held a security council seat four times, is competing against Portugal and Sweden for two of the temporary seats. A vote is expected at the end of October.
